title: School music and singing at the statue; poems for her daughters
summary: Music in public and Catholic school, singing at the statue, her Golden Age singing, and more poems dedicated to daughters.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: That's why I was going to ask you about your education what kind of music they taught you know in schools. Did they teach classical music or jazz or religious music?
Well I went to ferocious schools that would be mostly religious.
Mostly religious music that they were teaching. But you did get training on your instrument.

Oh and early up to the fifth grade I went to public school and we was taught other music and other songs you see. When I went to public school we used to go to make down a statue and make fun of day and bring flowers. Up to the fifth grade I went to public and then I left and from then on I went through a parocial. Then I went to Redemptus and finished there. Did you sing when you brought those flowers to the statue? We sang. I used to sing in the choir. I used to like to sing. Next time they have something at the Golden Age I'm going up on stage with them and sing. They wanted me to go last time but I was short of funds and they all had to have a certain costume and I couldn't look as good as they did so that's why I didn't have it. But when you see Walt Disney, the balls is going to come. You see the Golden Age balls and the costume and beautiful. But we had the Nord two weeks ago at the city park and a lady on the next block wanted me to go but I couldn't get a costume. And she has a husband and all and she could buy it and have it made and I didn't have the money to have it done. So I promised her that the next time I have something I'm going to find a way to have a costume. And we sing at the meetings and what's the matter with you? You can sing. Why don't you come with us? So two weeks ago they really sang and they really got clapping. Commissioner Shero congratulated them on the skit they put on. It really was good.
What did you sing when you went up to McDonald's statue?
Oh we'd sing a song that was dedicated to McDonald's. I don't exactly remember. We'd sing that old song Maryland, my Maryland. That used to be a wonder song.
But that was with the McDonald's words. Yeah. That was with McDonald's words. I remember that and I can't remember the words.
Maryland, my Maryland. Oh, John McDonough.
Oh, John McDonough. It goes something like that.

Yeah. We used to sing Stars Bang Havana of course. That's the first song we sang in praise to our flag. We'd all have flowers and every year they still do that. They go off Dr. McDonald's statue. Here's a poem. One I dedicated to my daughter Yvonne. That other one was to my daughter Effie, my little girl. Appreciation. This was written in 1951 I wrote this. And this book has been gone over by a critic. If you see the corrections. Everything's criticized. And told me he's ready for publication. And after that woman done me that I got the cold feet. Because I had no journalism or college. Oh, so much is meant by this void. To said people die of broken hearts. But I do believe it is for lack of appreciation and love. One is usually happy who is appreciated. And the more we appreciate others. The better we feel. I do want you to know I love you. And you appreciate the help, kindness, and happiness you do give me. God bless you and yours. Dedicated to my wonderful daughter Yvonne. This is dedicated to my oldest daughter Ayona. And this was to Ashley again. She was my baby. My baby. A while I held her in my arms. A helpless babe with all her charms. Until she grew so very fast. And baby ways too soon would pass. And when her baby smile had fled. I saw a little girl instead. Who sometimes fought to have her way. And so she grew from day to day. To crown by glorious womanhood. A happy bride before me stood. But timeless miracle had wrought. But I still hold the self-same thought. She's still my laugh and carefully held. And I as always tell myself. She's a baby still to me. And oh I know she'll always be. This is on the poetry exhibits. In 1951 and 1952. And I was also on radio with this poem. And read it. And on the Jackson Square we had this on the fence. This was on the 1951 and 1952. In the French Quarter. On the Jackson Square we had a march up and down. To hear the praise given our. Poetry and this one woman blasted all my hopes. I might have been a great portrait by now. Living in a swell place. This is one that went over big. I thought it did. I wrote this to Roland I believe when he was in the armed forces. A song in everything. There is a song in everything. In every little joy that comes. In babies as they suck their thumbs. The gay notes that the blue voids sing. The mother's patient gentle smile. The glory of the after while. There is no sadness but seems sweet with fragrance. And there is no day but speaks some beauty on life's way. The dusty and the weary feet upon their homeward journey. Bring the lights. The loving hearts may sing. The high chair in the cradle too. Have ever set brave lips to song. No grief has ever lived so long. But turned to music as it grew. And every hour of strife and pain. Leaves in the heart some sweet refrain. Lord teach me this from day to day. To find beyond the heightened care. Thy mercy shining everywhere. That it may brighten life's way. That went over very big.
